item.title: 10 Practical Ways to Broaden Your Perspective
item.description:
Resilience

10 Practical Ways to Broaden Your Perspective

Our perspective shapes the way we see and interact with the world.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • Perspective helps us make what matters most matter most.
  • Our perspective grows in relation to our lived experience.
  • We can build perspective intentionally through curiosity, reflection, and small daily practices.

Sometimes changing our perspective changes our entire experience. Imagine you're running late. Your shoulders climb toward your ears, your jaw tightens, and suddenly every red light feels personal. Now imagine you're driving that same route to share wonderful news. Same road, same traffic, same amount of time in the car, but an entirely different experience. The situation did not change. The lens did.

As I write about this pillar of Everyday Resiliency in my first book, Calm Within the Storm, “Our perspective is a constellation of attitudes, mindsets, and emotions that form a lens through which we see the world.” (Hanley-Dafoe, 2021, p. 124). It grows in relation to our lived experiences. Developing and practicing an integrated perspective helps us manage challenges, mitigate the impact of stressors, and open the door to learning and growth.

Perspective lets us see and feel our way through the world, show up in the hard parts, and prioritize what truly matters in the big picture.

A Little but Mighty Perspective Shift

One of my favourite perspective shifts happened a few summers ago.

My son Hunter and I had travelled to watch his younger brother, Jaxson, play in a basketball tournament. After warm-ups, we noticed Jaxson taking off his shoes and sitting down on the bench. When I went to investigate, I learned he had left his jersey at the hotel, and his coach's rule was firm: no player plays without the full uniform.

I immediately felt something that many high-performers struggle with: helplessness. My mind was already racing through ways to somehow get him into the second half when Hunter looked over and asked, “Mama, can I offer you some advice?” Thankfully, I leaned in to listen. He said, “Mama, this is going to be a bad hour. It's not a bad day. It's not a bad tournament. And it is absolutely not a bad life. This is just going to be a bad hour, and you're just going to have to find a way to sit with that, and, Mama, I promise you Jaxson will never forget a jersey again.”

I have shared that story countless times since because I think many of us need that reminder. Our brains are remarkably good at taking one difficult moment and writing an entire future around it. In this life, we will all have bad hours. My hope for you is that they stay exactly that.

That kind of moment, where the right piece of information lands at the right time, is what I think of as an unlock. It is a perspective shift that changes everything that comes after it, allowing us to move forward in a way we did not realize we needed.

Ways to Build and Expand Perspective

  1. Get curious: Perspective grows every time we are exposed to different ideas, people, and experiences. Read books written by people whose lives look different from yours. Listen to podcasts that challenge you. Ask someone, "Tell me more," and listen to understand rather than just waiting to respond. Curiosity stretches perspective.
  2. Zoom in, zoom out: When something feels overwhelming, zoom in first. Name what's happening and feel what you're feeling. Then zoom out. Ask yourself, “Will this matter in a week?” “In a year?” “How does this fit into the bigger story of my life?” Distress narrows our focus until everything feels urgent. Perspective helps us respond to what is important versus simply reacting to what feels loud.
  3. Notice the stories you are telling yourself: The way we narrate our own lives becomes the perspective we live inside of. “I'm a bad sleeper” is a very different sentence than “I'm someone who can sleep well under the right conditions.” The facts of the night might be identical. The story you carry forward is not.
  4. Collect evidence: Our brains naturally collect evidence that confirms what we already believe. If we believe we're failing, we'll notice every mistake. If we believe we're making progress, we'll start noticing growth. When you catch yourself telling a difficult story, try asking yourself, “What evidence supports this?” and “What evidence challenges it?” Perspective grows when we consider the whole picture, not just the pieces our brain highlights first.
  5. Change your physical view: Sometimes changing your physical perspective helps to change your mental one. Get outside, stand under the big sky, walk beside water, look out over a landscape. There is something about being reminded of how vast the world is that helps us right-size many of our worries.
  6. Borrow someone else's perspective: Sometimes we're standing too close to the problem. Ask a trusted friend, “What am I missing?” or “Help me think this through.” The people who love us can often see possibilities that we've temporarily lost sight of ourselves.
  7. Practice the power of "yet": The attitude we bring to our learning and challenges is extremely important. For example, “I don’t know how to do this” and “I don’t know how to do this yet” send our brain two very different messages. "Yet" leaves room for growth, learning, and hope.
  8. Recognize dual truths: Our brains are hardwired to focus on the negative, and in the midst of life's storms, that makes perspective genuinely hard to hold onto. Perspective expands when we stop believing we have to choose between two competing truths. For example, you can be disappointed and proud of how hard you tried. You can be grieving and grateful. You can feel uncertain and hopeful.
  9. Try “Unfortunately... Fortunately...”: This has become a family favourite of ours. It allows us to hold two truths at the same time, without pretending the hard part is not hard. Unfortunately, I'm stuck in traffic. Fortunately, I get more time to listen to my favourite podcast. Unfortunately, the presentation didn't go the way I'd hoped. Fortunately, I know exactly what I'll do differently next time.
  10. Build a gratitude practice: Our first thoughts of the day are the most powerful thoughts for the day. As soon as you are conscious or awake, say “Thank you.” Waking up to a new day is something to be grateful for. Then take a moment to hold space for what you have and what you get to do today.
article continues after advertisement

Final Thoughts

Every day we have opportunities to zoom in with honesty and zoom out with wisdom. We can get a little more curious, gently challenge the stories our brains automatically tell us, and remember that one bad hour is exactly that: an hour. Perspective widens what we can see and what feels possible. It helps us make what matters most matter most.

item.title: Are You a Segmenter or an Integrator?
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Are You a Segmenter or an Integrator?

Knowing the difference might be the key to improving your leadership.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • Great leaders don't assume that their way of working is best for everyone.
  • Employees differ on whether they are segmenters or integrators.
  • Segmenters prefer to keep work and life separate.
  • Integrators prefer to mix work and life tasks together.

Many leaders erroneously assume that their employees should structure work in the same way they do if they want to be successful. The truth is that employees’ ideal work styles and preferences differ. In our research, we find that great leaders recognize these differences and use them to maximize their team’s results. Weaker leaders are more stubborn, coaxing followers to adopt their ways of working without considering whether that’s actually what’s best. One key way that employees differ is with regard to whether they are segmenters or integrators. Before we outline how leaders take these preferences into account, it’s important to define these terms.

What are segmenters and integrators?

First, what are segmenters? Segmenters prefer to separate their work and life, while minimizing cross-domain interruptions (i.e., life tasks interrupting work, or vice versa). Segmenters like to work for a set number of hours and then move on to tackle life tasks and responsibilities. For example, a segmenter might block time from 7am-9am to get their kids ready and off to school, block 9am-5pm to work, and then close their laptop at 5pm to focus on making dinner, helping their children with homework, and watching television. Segmenters not only prefer to structure their work day so that work and life are separated, but they also experience more frustration when work interrupts life (or life interrupts work). So, if a segmenter has a sick child at home who needs care and attention during their work hours, this experience will feel more disruptive than it would to others with a weaker preference for segmentation.

Second, integrators prefer to mesh their work and life together, without trying to avoid (or even while trying to encourage) interruptions from either domain. Integrators prefer to alternate between work and life tasks, without creating clear boundaries between them. For example, an integrator might join a work call on the way home from dropping their kids off at school, pay bills online in between meetings, or do some laundry while listening to a work-related webinar. In contrast to segmenters, integrators don’t experience as much frustration when being interrupted by life tasks while working, or vice versa. Going back to our example of caretaking for a sick child during work hours, integrators would experience this disruption as less frustrating than a segmenter would.

Some employees prefer to enact strict boundaries between their work and life.
Source: Jan van der Wolf/Pexels

How can leaders support team members’ segmentation and integration preferences?

While most teams include members who are segmenters alongside those who are integrators, leaders don’t always account for these differences. Instead, they tend to assume that all of their team members share their preferences for segmentation or integration. Worse, some believe that team members should share their preferences and see their way of working as being the sole pathway to success.

However, excellent leaders don’t make these assumptions. Instead of trying to force team members to work in the same way they do, these leaders recognize that employees may benefit from a more tailored approach. More specifically, these leaders demonstrate key behaviors to learn their employees’ preferences and to enact a team culture that values them.

First, these leaders ask questions about employees’ preferred ways of working. For example, they might share whether they are an integrator or a segmenter and ask their employees which is their own preferred way of working. Second , after learning which style of working their employee prefers, great leaders take this into account via their leadership style. For instance, if a leader is an integrator and their team member is a segmenter, they might be tempted to contact them during off hours. However, great leaders will take steps to avoid doing so, as they know it will negatively impact their employees’ well-being and performance. In an effort to allow segmenters to disconnect, leaders might also schedule emails so that they arrive during work hours, instead of early or late when the leader might find it convenient to work. Further, they might try to avoid scheduling standing meetings before or after the workday ends (i.e., a meeting starting at 8:30am or ending at 5:30pm).

Other employees prefer to mix work and life tasks together throughout the day. What is your preference?
Source: Mikhail Nilov/Pexels

Similarly, if a leader is a segmenter and their employee is an integrator, they should recognize the automatic negative reaction they may have to employees who run errands or complete household chores during work hours. In turn, they might provide flexibility during the work day and focus more heavily on whether key deliverables and milestones were achieved on the whole. Overall, excellent leaders recognize that—as long as the work gets done (and the workload is reasonable)—when it gets done is less important.

Conclusion

Are you a segmenter or an integrator? How about your team members? If you’re unsure, you should ask them. Understanding their work preferences and recognizing how they match or mismatch with your own can spark meaningful dialogue that will improve your leadership. Whether you’re a segmenter or an integrator, it’s important to recognize that there is no one “correct” way to manage work and life. Instead, allowing employees to work in a way that supports their success and happiness is a win-win for everyone.

item.title: How to Build Sustainable Resilience in Creative Work
item.description:
Career

How to Build Sustainable Resilience in Creative Work

Learn to separate self-worth from rejection, visibility, and financial pressure.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • Creative work can blur the line between professional feedback and personal worth.
  • Visibility can create opportunity while also increasing exposure to judgment and rejection.
  • Financial confidence depends on boundaries, self-valuation, and asking to be paid fairly.
  • Resilience is healthier when it includes recovery, choice, and sustainable working conditions.
Creative work can bring meaning and autonomy, but it can also make rejection, visibility, and financial uncertainty feel deeply personal.
Source: Andrea Piacquadio / Pexels

Creative work is often romanticized as freedom.

The artist chooses the subject. The filmmaker tells the story. The musician follows a calling. From the outside, creative work can appear expressive, self-directed, and deeply meaningful.

But it also makes unusual psychological demands. When your work carries your identity, criticism can feel personal. When visibility is essential to success, being seen can also feel threatening. And when income is uncertain, questions about pricing can become entangled with questions of self-worth.

Earlier this month, women working across film, visual art, and music gathered at Henley Business School (disclosure: where I work) for Women in the Creative Industries: Resilience, Leadership, and Success, an event organized by the Centre for Euro-Asian Studies.

The discussions explored professional identity, visibility, financial sustainability, and the pressure to continue creating through uncertainty. Beneath them sat a broader psychological question: What does resilience mean when your work, income, and sense of self are so closely connected?

Resilience is often misunderstood. It is not the ability to absorb unlimited pressure without changing. Nor should it become a polite way of telling people to tolerate precarious, exclusionary, or poorly governed industries.

A better way to understand resilience is as a renewable psychological capacity. It can be strengthened, depleted, and restored.

Creative Work Makes the Self Part of the Product

In many jobs, criticism is directed at a task. In creative work, it can feel directed at the person.

A rejected proposal, poor review, empty gallery or unresponsive audience may be interpreted not simply as “this work did not succeed,” but as “I am not good enough.”

The boundary between performance and identity becomes thin.

Creative work often expresses how people see the world, what they value and who they understand themselves to be. That connection can be deeply motivating. It can also make setbacks harder to contain.

The psychological task is to remain invested in the work without becoming entirely defined by its reception. A creative identity requires commitment, but it also needs enough distance to survive rejection, revision, and silence.

This does not mean becoming emotionally detached. It means learning to separate the value of the self from the outcome of a particular project.

Visibility Is Both Necessary and Threatening

Creative professionals are regularly told to become more visible.

They must promote their work, communicate their value, develop networks and make themselves easier to discover. Yet visibility also brings exposure. It increases the possibility of criticism, comparison, and rejection.

This creates an approach-avoidance conflict. The person wants the opportunities that visibility may produce while fearing what being seen might cost.

Women can experience this tension particularly sharply when ambition, authority, or self-promotion conflicts with expectations about how they should behave.

They may be encouraged to speak confidently, then judged for appearing too forceful. They may be told to promote their achievements while also being expected to remain modest. They may be urged to price their work assertively while receiving signals that commercial ambition weakens artistic authenticity.

The answer is not simply to tell people to become braver. Hesitation may be a rational response to contradictory social demands.

What helps is controlled exposure: choosing where to be visible, deciding what to share, and refusing the idea that professional seriousness requires constant public availability.

Money Is Psychological Too

Financial instability is often treated as separate from creative identity. It is not.

Pricing work, negotiating fees and discussing income can activate questions of personal worth. A creative professional may struggle to distinguish between the market value of a commission and their value as a person.

This can contribute to underpricing, unpaid labor and chronic overextension. It can also create shame, particularly when meaningful work does not generate reliable income.

Financial confidence is therefore not only about spreadsheets. It involves boundaries, self-valuation and the ability to tolerate the discomfort of asking to be paid fairly.

A sustainable creative career requires both meaning and material viability. Treating money as somehow impure does not protect creativity. It can make creative people easier to exploit.

Resilience Is Not Endless Endurance

The creative industries often celebrate the person who keeps going.

Persistence becomes evidence of commitment. The artist works through exhaustion. The filmmaker accepts another unpaid opportunity. The musician keeps saying yes because the next break might matter.

But persistence is not always evidence of health. Sometimes it shows that someone has learned to ignore depletion.

Real resilience includes recovery. It may mean resting, changing direction, declining unpaid work, building another source of income or setting a boundary around availability.

It can also mean recognizing that the problem is not always personal.

Coaching, mentoring, and reflection can help people recover perspective, but they should not become substitutes for fair pay, inclusive leadership, transparent selection processes, or psychologically safe working conditions.

Recovering Agency

A useful starting point is to separate the work from the self.

Instead of asking, “What does this rejection say about me?” ask, “What information does this give me about the work, the audience, or the opportunity?”

It also helps to distinguish courage from overexposure. Visibility should be strategic, not compulsory.

Financial decisions should be treated as part of creative practice too. Pricing, negotiating, and protecting time are not distractions from the work. They are ways of making the work sustainable.

Three questions may help:

  1. What part of my identity has become too dependent on external approval?
  2. Where am I confusing endurance with resilience?
  3. What boundary, financial decision, or act of visibility would make my work more sustainable?

The goal is not to become harder to damage. It is to become better able to notice strain, restore capacity, protect identity, and decide what should happen next.

item.title: 5 Myths That Keep Emotional Neglect Hidden
item.description:
Child Development

5 Myths That Keep Emotional Neglect Hidden

The myths even professionals believe, and why they leave people stuck.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional neglect is one of the least understood childhood experiences, even among professionals.
  • It is not abuse; abuse is what a parent does, while neglect is what a parent fails to do.
  • It is not about how many parents you had or whether your parents loved you.
  • Because it’s quiet and easy to forget, its effects can be even more pernicious, yet they can be healed.
Source: JenkoAtaman/StockAdobe

Of the hundreds of psychological and emotional conditions, childhood emotional neglect is, in my opinion, among the least widely understood.

That's because we have spent decades talking about and studying the negative things that can happen to a child. As we've done all of this vital and important work, we have overlooked, and essentially ignored, an equal but opposite force: what fails to happen for a child.

Childhood emotional neglect is a parent's failure to respond enough to a child's emotional needs.

Here are five natural, automatic assumptions that are frequently held and expressed, even by mental health professionals.

Myth 1: Emotional neglect is a form of child abuse

This has been the default assumption of many people for many years. In professional articles and research studies, emotional neglect is typically lumped in with the various forms of child abuse. It's assumed that all of these forms of childhood mistreatment belong in the same category and have similar effects upon the child.

Yet nothing could be further from the truth. While abuse is a parental act, something a parent does to a child, emotional neglect is a parent's failure to act. The emotionally neglectful parent may never hit the child or call them a name. A mother (or father) simply fails to notice or respond enough to their child's emotional needs.

Not only does emotional neglect happen differently, but it also has different and distinct effects. Since the causes and effects of emotional neglect are all different from abuse, the path to healing is also different.

Myth 2: It happens more often in single-parent, divorced, or widowed families

Contrary to how logical this assumption may seem, it's not at all true. Emotional neglect is not about the number of available parents or even the time available to spend with parents. It's a matter of the emotional quality of the parent/child connection. Does the parent truly know the child on a deeply personal, emotional level? Does the parent notice, validate, and respond to the child's feelings? Does the parent teach the child how to tolerate, manage, and express their emotions? These emotional aspects of parenting are not necessarily related to whether a parent is single or married.

article continues after advertisement

In fact, many single parents are aware that their single parenthood, divorce, or loss has affected their children, and take extra care to notice what their children are feeling and to support them.

Myth 3: It is not as damaging as abuse

It is true that emotional neglect causes a different set of challenges than the experience of childhood abuse. But it's not true that the effects of abuse are worse.

Emotional neglect is a quieter, less visible childhood experience than abuse, so, as you might expect, its effects are quieter and less visible. But this is also what makes its effects more pernicious. Those who experience abuse will be impacted by it. They will grow up feeling perhaps violated, unsafe, and mistrusting. They may struggle to feel emotionally (or even physically) safe in relationships.

The effects of emotional neglect are more like carrying around a weight. The emotionally neglected child must push away their emotions. In adulthood, they lack access to this highly connecting, grounding, and enriching part of their life. They then find themselves living in a gray world, feeling alone. Since they likely can't recall the subtle and invisible emotional neglect from their childhood, they feel innately flawed. They assume that they are to blame for these struggles.

Myth 4: Emotional neglect results from a lack of love from your parents

Ironically, it's often the most loving parents who emotionally neglect their children. This is because love and emotional attention are not the same thing and do not necessarily go together.

In my experience, the single factor that most predicts a parent's likelihood of emotionally neglecting their children is not whether they love their children. It's having been raised with emotional neglect herself.

article continues after advertisement

Myth 5: All therapists know about it and how to treat it

Virtually every therapist understands the foundation of emotional neglect: that when a child's emotional needs are not met, the child will suffer negative effects into adulthood.

However, there is far more to emotional neglect than this general foundational point. What are the specific effects of emotional neglect? Exactly how and why do they happen? How do you know when a patient has it? How do you treat it specifically? The answers to these questions are not common knowledge in the professional mental health community.

Once You Can See It

Childhood emotional neglect is real. When your parents fail to respond sufficiently to your emotional needs, it does not matter why. It leaves a mark on you as you grow into your adulthood. This mark you share with others who grew up in a similar way. This mark can be healed.

Emotional neglect can be invisible when it happens, and also hard to remember once you grow up. But once you see it clearly, you can begin to set it right.

A version of this post also appears on emotionalneglect.com © Jonice Webb, Ph.D.

item.title: Yas Queen! Drag and Trans Women’s Mental Health
item.description:
Gender

Yas Queen! Drag and Trans Women’s Mental Health

The history and mental health benefits of drag performance for trans women.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • Drag was founded by trans women of color in New York City’s ballroom scene.
  • A recent academic study found that drag was related to improved mental health outcomes for trans women.
  • Drag helps trans individuals to explore gender fluidity, find community, and experience gender affirmation.

This post was co-authored with Abigail Tessmer.

Protests like Compton’s Cafeteria Riots and the Stonewall Uprising have become meaningful symbols of LGBTQ resistance against police harassment and violence. What is often left out of these stories, however, is the central role that Black and Brown trans women, femmes, and drag queens played in them. They faced the harshest police violence and were among the first to push back. Despite their leadership, many were excluded from mainstream LGBTQ+ activist groups and rewritten in the history they helped create. The irony is hard to miss: While white cisgender gay and lesbian individuals were gaining civil rights, gender-diverse people of color were stigmatized as “deviant others” in need of carceral interventions.

Source: Oriel Frankie Ashcroft/Pexels

In response, Black and Brown trans women, femmes, and drag artists created their own spaces throughout the 1980s and 1990s. One of the most influential was the ballroom scene. These were gender-fluid spaces where drag performers formed “houses” of chosen families and competed against one another in a “ballroom” (usually a warehouse or abandoned space). Each ball was themed, requiring different types of dress and performance for categories that highlighted and celebrated femininity and queerness, with the hopes of “snatching” trophies and gaining status.

These ballroom houses—typically led by a trans woman or femme “mother”—were spaces that provided drag performers with what society often denied them: family, housing, support, guidance, and a sense of belonging. They were places where trans and gender-diverse people could survive, thrive, and celebrate one another.

Drag Goes Mainstream

By the early 2000s, drag was reaching mainstream audiences in ways it never had before. Shows like RuPaul’s Drag Race introduced drag to millions of viewers and helped transform it into a cultural phenomenon. But as drag gained popularity, a familiar problem emerged: The very trans women and gender-diverse people who helped build drag culture were once again pushed to the sidelines.

For years, Drag Race solely featured gay cis (and mostly white) men as female impersonators, with misogynistic and transphobic “jokes” as punchlines for multiple recurring bits. Facing backlash for refusing to include trans women on the cast, RuPaul doubled down on his stance in 2018, comparing trans women on Drag Race to athletes “doping themselves” in the Olympics. Although the franchise has become more inclusive, many continue to emphasize that drag’s roots run much deeper than a televised competition. World-renowned gender-bending queens like Sasha Velour remind us that trans women of color have been doing drag for “literal centuries” and deserve representation, recognition, and respect.

Drag as we know it was created from the aesthetics, style, and brilliant imaginations of trans women and femmes of color, and they continue to elevate drag spaces all over the world today. These spaces operate as safe havens for many trans and gender diverse individuals and have shown to promote gender affirmation, garner community support, and improve mental health outcomes (Rogers, 2018).

Why We Investigated Drag and Mental Health

Source: SHOX ART/Pexels

When people hear the phrase “gender affirmation,” many think about medical care such as hormones or surgery. But gender affirmation can also occur in social and community settings. At its core, gender affirmation involves having one’s identity recognized, supported, and validated by others (Glynn et al., 2016).

The role of gender-affirming spaces like drag is especially relevant right now. At a time when trans people and drag artists are increasingly becoming targets of political manipulation and legislative restrictions, it’s worth asking what might be lost if these spaces disappear. Do drag spaces provide something meaningful for the health and well-being of trans people?

That question motivated our recent study published in The Journal of Creativity in Mental Health. We wanted to know whether drag could act as a form of gender affirmation. Given the deep historical connections between trans women and drag culture, we wondered: Does drag participation relate to better mental health outcomes for trans women? To explore this question, we used data from the 2015 U.S. Transgender Survey, the largest survey of trans people to-date with nearly 30,000 participants.

What We Found

The results were striking.

Compared to trans women who did not participate in drag, trans women who did participate in drag had significantly more positive mental health outcomes. And when compared to trans men and nonbinary drag performers, the positive effect of drag participation for trans women was more robust.

Why might that be? We believe drag promotes mental wellness by creating opportunities for gender exploration, creativity, affirmation, and connection. Drag allows people to experiment with and express different aspects of themselves in environments that are often far more supportive than their everyday surroundings.

For trans women who regularly encounter discrimination and violence (Tessmer and Worthen, 2025), drag spaces can offer something powerful: the freedom to explore gender without having to defend it. Through costumes, makeup, performance, fashion, and creativity, drag creates opportunities for self-expression that can foster confidence, joy, and ultimately, gender euphoria.

And the impact doesn’t stop when the show ends! The confidence, support, and gender affirmation found in drag spaces can carry over into other parts of life as well.

Source: Mayara Caroline Mombelli/Pexels

Why This Matters Right Now

Our findings suggest that drag is much more than a performance—it’s a mental health boost that should be valued as a legitimate mechanism for trans and gender-diverse individuals to creatively explore gender fluidity, find community, and experience gender affirmation.

That makes ongoing attacks on drag and trans communities particularly concerning. Since 2020, anti-trans legislation has increased dramatically and efforts to restrict drag performances have gained traction in many states. These policies limit access to the very spaces that many rely on for community, expression, and safety.

As researchers and activists, we encourage others to continue organizing, researching, and investing in queer and trans lives by attending drag shows and other events held by LGBTQ+ people, getting involved in political protests, citing and interacting with research written by and for queer and trans people, and creating safe spaces for queer and trans people.

item.title: Chronic Illness Is the New Rite of Passage in Motherhood
item.description:
Chronic Illness

Chronic Illness Is the New Rite of Passage in Motherhood

Personal Perspective: Changing the narrative around chronic illness and motherhood.

Posted July 24, 2026

This morning, I woke up at 6 a.m. and willingly went to an imaging center to allow them to shove my body into a metal tube and take pictures of all of my organs. The technician became interested in my reason for being there once I disclosed that I was six months postpartum. I explained my months-long journey, which included one endoscopy, two colonoscopies, a CT scan, multiple blood tests, and now an MRI (with insurance still refusing to cover the medication I need to not die), along with the joking warning: You'll be fine if you don't get pregnant.

She leaned over and said, "I just found out that I am."

At that point, I did everything I could to minimize. I had a higher risk. Autoimmunity runs in my family. I had unexplained symptoms from childhood. This would not happen to her.

Except it might.

She already has Hashimoto's, she disclosed, and, as she put it, autoimmune disorders run in packs.

As I sat still in that metal tube, listening to the whirring sounds of the machine and Carly Rae Jepsen blaring through the headphones (I asked for Taylor Swift), I couldn't help but think: Is this just a rite of passage into motherhood?

Two months after the birth of my second baby, I was diagnosed with Crohn's disease. The diagnosis was a long time coming and not much of a shock. I finished talking to the doctor, wandered out to the car to meet my husband and my baby, and then went about my business. I did not have time to process the new, and massively life-altering, diagnosis. There was work to do and two young boys who needed me.

As a therapist working in maternal mental health, I tend to work with perfectionism quite a bit. The women I work with are over-functioning, high-achieving, and often—quite sick. I see women with unexplained stomach issues, headaches, high blood pressure, and chronic pain, many of them far too young to be feeling so old.

This is not surprising. Women in the childbearing years often experience extreme physical and psychological demands associated with pregnancy, childbirth, and parenting. Approximately 80% of individuals diagnosed with autoimmune diseases are women, with many autoimmune conditions first emerging during the reproductive years (Angum, Khan, Kaler, Siddiqui, & Hussain, 2020). There is no denying that something about the state of being a woman, especially a mother, is making us sick. Research titled Neglected Medium- and Long-Term Consequences of Labour and Childbirth has shown that more than one-third of women will experience a long-term health condition after childbirth (Vogel et al., 2024).

Chronic illness feels like the price you have to pay to be a woman, much less a mother, in our culture. And now, the culture at large is trying to convince you that it is your fault.

There is a new and increasingly concerning dialogue around chronic health conditions that is not unfamiliar: It's all in your head—but not in the way that you think.

Spend a few minutes on TikTok or Instagram, and you'll quickly encounter messages suggesting that chronic illness is simply a manifestation of unresolved trauma or poor self-care. While I do not want to discredit the role that unresolved trauma and mental illness have on the body, when you dig deeper into this type of messaging, it is often a new form of ableism in disguise.

When I finally came to grips with my diagnosis, the underbelly was deep grief that took the form of a call and response:

I did everything right, so why did I get sick?

Then, immediately:

So, is your illness your fault for not living life right?

I realized that this is the same Puritan-drenched thinking that we all know so well.

When you start seeing this messaging, you see it everywhere. You see it in ads for anti-inflammatory diets. You see it in doctors' offices and from therapists on the internet. If you let go of your trauma, move your body, take this supplement, lose weight, go on a retreat, do a cleanse, start yoga, set small daily goals—you won't get sick. And if you do get sick, you should have lived differently. Try again next time.

While I do not think that repressed emotions cause chronic illness, I do think that we have to have a reckoning with the fact that our bodies cannot carry on this way and that we have to find a way to start listening to them.

This is where the conversation can become more productive.

While I don't think I caused my illness, I do think that it is forcing me to live my life differently. Living with chronic illness calls you to live differently. The over-functioning has to stop. The inflamed and exhausted body can no longer maintain the shoving down of emotions and people-pleasing. Perfectionism cannot live in a body that is inherently "imperfect," and there is something very freeing about that fact.

So, if there is anything to take away here, it would be this: Women are getting sick, and they are getting sick at a much higher rate than men. We should look into this. We need research to find ways to stop these conditions from occurring.

Living "wrongly" did not cause this, and living the "right way" will not fix it.

And yet, chronic illness is calling you to live differently.

Listen to your body. Pay attention to how you are talking to yourself. Notice how you are metabolizing emotions, and allow your priorities to shift as your body needs. Above all, allow yourself time to grieve and process.

Your life is not over, and in many ways, it may be just beginning.

item.title: A Minute of Advice Is Not Ten Years of Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

A Minute of Advice Is Not Ten Years of Therapy

A viral Mark Manson clip mistakes advice for psychological change.

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • Psychological insight can guide change, but lasting change requires practice, feedback, and repetition.
  • Therapy is more than advice. It helps people act differently when difficult thoughts and feelings appear.
  • The therapeutic relationship offers a real setting to notice, practice, and strengthen new ways of living.
  • Brief psychological content can help, but it should not be mistaken for years of therapeutic work.

A new genre of video has begun appearing in my social media feeds:

“Ten years of therapy summarized in one minute.”

“Forty-five years of therapy in sixteen minutes.”

“Everything my therapist taught me, explained in sixty seconds.”

The most widely shared version in my feed features self-help author Mark Manson and podcaster Chris Williamson. Williamson reads a seven-point list attributed to Manson with advice like "take responsibility for your life" and "establish strong boundaries". I have no quarrel with the list’s reasonably helpful principles.

But it is not ten years of therapy.

Mark Manson’s framing, when consumed in short-form video, reduces psychotherapy to advice delivery. Imagine a fitness influencer announcing, “Ten years of gym workouts summarized in one minute.” The video might say: Lift weights. Do cardio. Eat protein. Sleep well. Be consistent.

All reasonably helpful principles, but not remotely equivalent to ten years of training.

Knowing the principles of physical fitness does not produce strength, endurance, or cardiovascular capacity. Those emerge through repeated effort over time. You perform the exercises, tolerate discomfort, recover, and return.

Psychological change works in a functionally similar way.

Therapy Is Not a Transfer of Secret Information

These videos often rest on a mistaken assumption: Therapy consists primarily of a professional telling a client important things. It suggests that after years of going to therapy, the client has accumulated a collection of profound lessons. The influencer can now reveal the best ones in under a minute, saving everyone else years of time and money. That is not how effective therapy works.

Most therapists are not guarding a vault containing the secret sentences that will finally help the person understand what they are struggling. Across more than 30 years of helping people with Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, Functional Analytic Psychotherapy, and other evidence-based interventions, I have found that many clients already understand a great deal about what they are struggling with.

As an old psychodynamic supervisor of mine used to say, “Insight and a buck-and-a-quarter will get you on the subway.” That line also tells you how long ago he said it.

The difficulty is rarely an absolute shortage of information. The difficulty is learning to behave differently when fear, shame, grief, anger, craving, uncertainty, or old habits show up.

That cannot be accomplished in sixty seconds.

Insight Is Not the Same as Learning

A person may have an important realization during therapy. Sometimes a therapist offers a phrase, metaphor, or question that stays with someone for decades. But even a powerful insight is usually the beginning of the work, not its conclusion.

Consider the advice to “set boundaries.” That sounds simple until setting a boundary means disappointing your mother, confronting your employer, risking conflict with your partner, or being willing to experience that someone may think poorly of you. That requires practice.

An aphorism says, “Set a boundary.” Therapy asks: Which boundary? With whom? What do you fear will happen? How can we practice this new commitment, and what are you going to do when the first attempt doesn’t turn out as planned?

A one-minute video can tell you to set a boundary. Therapy helps you uncover what makes that difficult, practice it with feedback, and refine it until it becomes usable in your life.

To give another analogy, a cooking video can explain how to make candied bacon cashews for Thanksgiving dessert. Watching it does not mean you have developed the skill.

Manson Actually Helps Make the Point

To his credit, Manson becomes considerably more nuanced in the longer podcast conversation. He says that earlier in his career he believed personal growth was mainly about finding a few crucial pieces of information. He now thinks the principles are often already familiar and that people need consistent rituals and reminders to keep them present in daily life.

Therapy Also Happens Between People

The “therapy in one minute” format minimizes another central ingredient of treatment: the therapeutic relationship.

For many clients, therapy provides an unusual interpersonal environment. They can speak honestly, observe how they relate to another person, receive feedback, experience disagreement without abandonment, and practice behaving differently in real time.

Sometimes, more simply, they can have someone safe to cry in front of.

As I learned from Mavis Tsai and Robert Kohlenberg, the originators of Functional Analytic Psychotherapy, the relationship is not incidental packaging around therapeutic wisdom. It can be an active context in which change is noticed, shaped, and practiced.

The Problem Is Not Brevity

I am not opposed to concise psychological education. I have spent much of my career trying to explain complicated behavioral principles clearly. Sometimes I am even successful at it.

A short video can introduce a valuable idea. It can normalize an experience, teach a coping strategy, challenge a misconception, or encourage someone to seek help.

The problem is the grandiose framing.

“Here is one idea I learned in therapy” is honest.

“This concept changed how I think about anxiety” is plausible.

“Ten years of therapy in one minute” implies that treatment is mostly bloated explanation—and that years of professional work can be replaced by a clever monologue delivered over dramatic music.

It also encourages the fantasy that transformation should be immediate. When viewers understand the message but continue behaving in familiar ways, they may conclude that they are weak, resistant, or broken. They may scroll through hundreds of short-form videos, continue to suffer, and take that as evidence that something is fundamentally wrong with them.

There may be nothing mysterious about it. Understanding something quickly and learning to live it are different achievements.

Therapy Should Still Be Accountable

None of this means that more therapy is always better. Treatment should have clear, values-based goals. Therapists should measure and evaluate whether their work is helping. Some clients benefit from brief interventions. Remaining in ineffective treatment for ten years is not an accomplishment.

Clinical psychology should be challenged when it becomes vague, stagnant, unnecessarily prolonged, or detached from evidence.

But the alternative to bad therapy is not pretending that psychological change can be reduced to a TikTok video.

The One-Minute Version

So here is my attempt to summarize ten years of therapy in one sentence:

We learn to notice what is genuinely present here and now, recognize that we are bigger than our thoughts, feelings, and memories, choose what matters, practice living it, and use feedback—including the therapeutic relationship—to track whether our actions are moving us toward a more vital and meaningful life.

That sentence took less than a minute to read.

Now comes the part that takes time: doing it regularly.

That is why Siri Ming and I wrote Finding Your Why and Finding Your Way as a workbook: insight becomes useful through practice, not passive consumption.

A video can offer a direction. It cannot travel the distance for you.

A reel can point toward the gym. It cannot do the repetitions.

A one-minute insight may be genuinely valuable. It still is not ten years of therapy.

item.title: Narcissism and Romantic Relationships: Swallowing the Bitter Pill
item.description:
Relationships

Narcissism and Romantic Relationships: Swallowing the Bitter Pill

What is the secret to resolving the pesky and persistent repetition compulsion?

Posted July 24, 2026

Key points
  • Neurotic narcissism undermines many intimate relationships.
  • Repetition compulsion is driven by a wounded inner child hoping for a different outcome.
  • Confronting and grieving the past frees us to live more freely in the present.

This post is Part 4 of a series.

Many people have an uncanny attraction, a kind of unconscious radar or heat-seeking missile, for members of the opposite sex (or sometimes same sex) who blatantly or subtly resemble—psychologically if not physically—the parent with whom they had difficulties. And these are the people we tend to “fall in love” with or with whom we become romantically involved. The parallels are usually imperceptible at first (to ourselves though not to others), becoming more apparent as the relationship progresses. We choose such people unconsciously and unwittingly. That is the very nature of a neurosis. It’s a “blind spot” or a complex. Who in their right mind would consciously choose—or remain with—a partner who is rejecting, unavailable, or abusive? That would be pure masochism. But it is much more than masochism. It is a powerful unconscious repetition compulsion at play. (See my prior post.)

The Wounded Inner Child

That wounded, rejected, abandoned little boy or girl within us is still vying to win mommy or daddy’s love. In order for the repetition compulsion to play out, the love interest must, by definition, possess at least some of the emotional deficits or traits as the original parent. Indeed, that is what the repetition compulsion is all about: an unconscious recreation or recapitulation of these relationship dynamics, so as to provide an opportunity to alter the outcome. The needy inner child thinks: “This time will be different. I will get this new person to love me. I can change him or her, if only I try hard enough. I won’t fail again. I will make them love me. Then I will finally feel loveable and worthy of love.”

But tragically, this futile effort is doomed to failure. For if, as part of the repetition compulsion, we specifically choose individuals who cannot love us precisely because of their own emotional limitations and problems, what are the chances of them doing so? Can we “fix” them? Force them? Transform them? Cure them? Not very likely. The rational, intellectual adult part of ourselves knows this. But the wounded little boy or girl within is still striving to do so, just as he or she previously tried with the parents. And the vicious cycle continues. Such relationships will not work —they cannot, despite our best efforts. Each inevitable failure triggers and reinforces deep-seated feelings of inadequacy, inferiority, and unlovability. And so it goes.

The "Bitter Pill"

So what is the secret to resolving the pesky and persistent repetition compulsion? Are we doomed to repeat the same mistakes ad nauseum? Not necessarily. This knotty problem can be gradually disentangled, but always with great difficulty. That's because it requires relinquishing the compulsive defense mechanism itself. The repetition compulsion has a basic survival function. It defends against the re-experiencing of all those overwhelmingly painful feelings we denied during childhood about our imperfect parents and ourselves: sadness, anger, rage, despair, hopelessness, and hurt.

These were narcissistic injuries. They were emotions that we were environmentally and developmentally unprepared and unable to cope with at that time, and that we continued avoiding into adulthood, but that we must now finally confront. These are frightening metaphorical demons we must summon the courage to face — not just cognitively or intellectually, but experientially. The childish hope and denial that once kept us afloat and sane in a raging sea of sadness must now be surrendered, and reality accepted: Tragically, our natural infantile or childhood dependency needs for love, affection, understanding, acceptance, caring, etc. were never adequately met, and they never will be. Why? Because that time in our lives is over, ancient history, and can never be relived. What happened, sadly, happened. The bell cannot be unrung. What was done cannot be undone. To persist in hoping for this to happen is to be stuck in the past. As Breuer and Freud (1895) once said, we "suffer mainly from reminiscences," which prevents us from fully living in the present and future.

I call this critical turning point in treatment the “bitter pill.” And I am not talking here about some new medication! But the “bitter pill” is nonetheless strong emotional stuff, so one needs to be psychologically prepared and ready to swallow it: Never will we receive from our parents (or anyone, for that matter) all we needed. Nothing can ever change that. This is an agonizing and infuriating loss that must at last be fully acknowledged, grieved, mourned, and accepted in order to get past it. The secret to doing so, as I’ve elsewhere suggested (1996), “entails the mature acceptance of the traumatic facts of one’s emotional mortification, the causes and consequences, as well as a resolute willingness to swallow the following bitter pill: We cannot change the past nor undo the wound. . . We can, nonetheless, allow ourselves to feel our rage and grief over this irretrievable loss. . . . We may even—with some good fortune, time and grace—find within ourselves the capacity to forgive those whom we feel inflicted our agonizing injuries.” (p. 286)

With this courageous, conscious acceptance, confrontation, and coming to terms with the past, the repetition compulsion, like the past itself, loses its disastrous domination over us in the present. The spell is at last dispelled. The unconscious curse is lifted. The bewitchment is broken. We gradually grow more free to create new and different relationships. Relationships that, rather than repeatedly ravaging and re-wounding us, nourish, replenish, and restore our soul.
